body: Home / Plan Your Trip / Add Stops to Your Route Add Stops to Your Route Riding a route you already have? title: Be Prepared
desc: What's worth knowing before a bike trip in BC, most important first: emergencies and cell coverage, road and trail conditions, wildlife, rules of the road, and how to be a good guest.
body: Home / Plan Your Trip / Be Prepared Be prepared BC is big, wild, and gloriously empty in places. That's exactly why you're coming. It also means a little preparation goes a long way. Here's what's worth knowing before you roll out, most important first. Winlaw, BC Weather moves fast in the mountains. Plan for it, then enjoy it. If something goes wrong # The emergency number everywhere in BC is 911 . It's the right first call for medical emergencies and for search and rescue. The catch: much of the province has zero cell service. Outside towns and highway corridors, assume your phone won't work. Download offline maps and a weather forecast whenever you have signal or wifi. For remote routes, consider a satellite layer: a Garmin inReach, an iPhone with satellite SOS, or Rogers Satellite, which works on recent phones from any carrier and covers most of BC south of the 58th parallel, outdoors with a view of the sky. Texting only, but texting 911 from a valley with no bars is the feature that matters. Before a multi-day trip, tell someone where you're going and when you'll be back. AdventureSmart calls this a trip plan, and their free tools make it a two-minute job. Stranded rather than hurt? A broken frame or unfixable flat is a logistics problem, not an emergency. BCAA members get Bike Assist, roadside help that covers bicycles anywhere a service vehicle can reach. title: How we describe routes
desc: What every route label on this site means, value by value: difficulty, comfort, surface, ruggedness, climbing, and remoteness, plus where the data comes from and how to tell us when it looks wrong.
body: Home / Get Inspired / How we describe routes How we describe routes Routes on this site come from many different publishers, and each one describes rides in its own words. One publisher’s “intermediate” is another’s “hard”, and many say nothing about traffic or surface at all. We encourage you to read how the publishers describe their own routes. To help you understand routes across publishers, here we describe every route ourselves, the same way, with the same labels. When two routes both say Mostly gravel , they mean the same thing. Here’s what each label means. Difficulty # Our overall read of how demanding a route is. We score surface roughness, climbing, singletrack, and how far it runs from services. The route publisher's own rating, a lot of busy road riding, or sheer scale can push the tier up, never down. Easy Smooth surfaces and gentle climbing. Moderate One step up. Some real climbing, or a rougher surface. Ambitious A real undertaking. Demanding on a couple of fronts, like rough surfaces plus steady climbing, or a long stretch on busier roads. Challenging Demanding on several fronts at once, or a lot of riding on busy roads. Epic Expedition scale. Many demanding factors stacked, or 1,000 km and up, or 10,000 m of climbing. Comfort # How much of the route you spend sharing the road with cars. Bike paths, quiet streets, and car free backcountry roads count as comfortable. Busy or fast roads don't. Photo: BIKEPACKING.com Bikepacking the Sea to Sky Trail Highlight Bikepacking the Sea to Sky Trail BIKEPACKING.com · 101 km · Weekend or more Challenging Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 14 km Mixed surface Lots of singletrack Lots of climbing The Sea to Sky Trail runs 101 km from Squamish through Whistler to Pemberton, tracing a corridor the Coast Salish and Interior Salish peoples travelled long before highways. Nearly half is flowy singletrack, and the rest mixes doubletrack, gravel, and pavement past turquoise lakes, swimming holes, suspension bridges, and even an old train wreck. Climbs come short and punchy rather than long. Resupply is easy in all three towns, and public transit can carry you back to the start. Guide by Miles Arbour and Nathan Reimer. Photo: BIKEPACKING.com Frog Peak Loop Highlight Frog Peak Loop BIKEPACKING.com · 107 km · Weekend or more Ambitious Some traffic sharing Mostly gravel Lots of climbing If you are going to convert a first-time bikepacker, this is the route: 107 km linking rail grade, scenic gravel, and sub-alpine lakes through the Slocan Valley, with the beloved Frog Peak Cafe on course and swimming holes for hot afternoons. It publishes original and curated bikepacking routes, gear reviews, adventure stories, and planning guides, with a global route network spanning nearly 50 countries, alongside a biannual print magazine, The Bikepacking Journal. Their BC collection bikepacking.com's British Columbia routes run from sub-100 km overnighters to multi-week expeditions such as the 1,164 km BC Trail and the roughly 1,046 km Tree to Sea Loop around northern Vancouver Island, with coverage across BC. Its route pages are unusually deep: full logistics (access, resupply, camping, difficulty) and absolutely beautiful photography. It has also singled out the West Kootenay as a destination-level bikepacking region, with a dedicated route network guide centred on Nelson (bikepacking.com/west-kootenay) linking the Kootenay Confluence, Santa Rosa Valleys and Vistas, Bonnington Scrambler, and Frog Peak Loop routes. Terrain is predominantly unpaved gravel and forest service road. 26 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. desc: Love Machine's complete BC cycling route collection — 16 rides — on Get Inspired, BC Cycle Tourism Society.
body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / Love Machine Love Machine individual route creator visit → Love Machine is a Vancouver-based gravel cycling project run by two friends, Max and Cam, as a side project — not a brand, shop, or club. It publishes free, downloadable GPX routes across southwestern British Columbia, with a stated goal of keeping gravel cycling welcoming rather than gatekept. Their BC collection Love Machine's routes cluster around Metro Vancouver, the North Shore, and the Sea-to-Sky corridor, from short urban gravel loops in Burnaby, Richmond, and North Vancouver to bigger days in Squamish, Golden Ears, and Cultus Lake, plus a Sunshine Coast overnighter and two Vancouver Island loops near Comox and Campbell River. Routes run 40-110 km on a mix of forest service roads and singletrack, often borrowing flow trails from the North Shore and Squamish mountain bike networks. 16 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. title: Trails BC
desc: Trails BC's complete BC cycling route collection — 12 rides — on Get Inspired, BC Cycle Tourism Society.
body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / Trails BC Trails BC trail organization visit → Trails BC (the Trails Society of BC) is a non-profit charity that advocates for greenway trails for self-propelled recreation and active transportation across the province. Léon Lebrun has been at the heart of that work for nearly three decades, building and championing non-motorized trails across the Lower Mainland and beyond; a bridge in Chilliwack and a trail in Port Moody now carry his name. The rides shown here are a handful of the many he's helped map over the years. Their BC collection Trails BC's routes here range from short 12 km community loops to a 220 km multi-day Kootenay loop, and include several short Trans Canada Trail feeder segments in the Fraser Valley (Chilliwack Lake to Thurston, Cultus Lake to Tamihi, Langley to Clayburn) alongside day loops around Salmo, Kaslo/Slocan, Kimberley, Nanaimo, Squamish, Summerland, and Chilliwack. Coverage spans Kootenay Rockies, Vancouver Coast and Mountains, Vancouver Island, and Thompson Okanagan, with terrain running from flat valley-bottom trail to sustained climbing (over 1,300 m and 2,300 m of ascent on the two longest Kootenay routes). 12 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. Their BC collection Bikepack Canada's British Columbia routes range from a 75 km alpine overnighter near Squamish to the 1,200 km Kootenay Flathead Fandango loop through BC, Montana, Idaho, and Washington. body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / Cross Canada Cycle Tour Society Cross Canada Cycle Tour Society touring organization visit → The Cross Canada Cycle Tour Society (CCCTS) is a non-profit cycling club founded in 1982, based in British Columbia with a chapter in Ottawa. In its own words, it is a club for active adults of all ages; members are mainly retired people who love recreational cycling. Volunteers organize weekly day rides plus multi-day and cross-Canada tours, some of which have run continuously since the 1980s. Their BC collection The Cross Canada Cycle Tour Society's BC routes range from short day rides of about 84 km to a 1,511 km cross-provincial tour toward Calgary. Most of its routes here are on Vancouver Island, with others in the Lower Mainland and Fraser Valley and one crossing northern British Columbia, the Cariboo-Chilcotin Coast, and the Thompson-Okanagan. Most routes are on paved roads with rolling-to-climbing terrain, and the set includes several multi-day touring routes and one route linked by four ferry crossings. 10 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / Adventure Cycling Association Adventure Cycling Association touring organization visit → For over 50 years, Adventure Cycling Association has been mapping the most iconic bike routes in North America, including the TransAmerica Trail and the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route. It hosts over 90,000 kilometres of bikepacking and bike touring routes, leads dozens of guided tours each year, and advocates to protect the routes, access, and infrastructure that make bike travel possible. Supported by members and donors, Adventure Cycling's nonprofit mission is to inspire, empower, and connect people to travel by bike. Their BC collection Adventure Cycling Association's routes touching British Columbia fall into two groups: multi-day bikepacking and touring loops around Greater Vancouver and Vancouver Island (paved and mixed surface, roughly 460-660 km), and long-distance touring and gravel routes through the Kootenay-Rockies and northern BC that continue into Alberta, Yukon, and the United States, including the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route, Great Parks North, Selkirk Splendor, and the Alaskan Golden Circle Tour. Terrain is mostly rolling, with surfaces ranging from fully paved to substantially unpaved gravel. Its flagship Pacific Coast route also touches BC, starting in Vancouver before running the length of the US West Coast. 6 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / British Columbia Randonneurs British Columbia Randonneurs cycling club visit → British Columbia Randonneurs Cycling Club is a long-distance cycling club with deep roots: randonneuring in BC dates to 1979, and the club was a founding member of Les Randonneurs Mondiaux, the world body for 1,200 km grand randonnées, in 1983. With regional chapters in the Lower Mainland, Vancouver Island, Southern Interior, and Peace Region, it organizes brevets (timed long-distance rides of 200 km and up), populaires (shorter introductory events), and permanents (self-paced routes available year-round), and publishes the routes on Ride with GPS. Its celebrated Rocky Mountain 1200 drew riders from around the world. Their BC collection The club's routes in this set are populaires of 100 to 160 km with 400 to 820 m of climbing over rolling terrain, on mostly paved roads with some mixed-surface sections. Two start in Metro Vancouver (Vancouver and Langley) and one on southern Vancouver Island (Saanich), consistent with the club's day-length, brevet-style long-distance riding format. 3 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. title: Trans Canada Trail
desc: Trans Canada Trail's complete BC cycling route collection — 2 rides — on Get Inspired, BC Cycle Tourism Society.
body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / Trans Canada Trail Trans Canada Trail trail organization visit → Trans Canada Trail is a national charitable organization, based in Ottawa, that coordinates and maintains the Trans Canada Trail (also known as The Great Trail) — a roughly 30,000 km multi-use trail network spanning every Canadian province and territory and connecting the Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic coastlines. The network supports hiking, cycling, paddling, and other activities, and is built and managed through partnerships with regional and local trail organizations rather than owned as a single continuous trail. Their BC collection Two Trans Canada Trail cycling routes cover British Columbia. The southern route runs about 1,768 km from the Kootenays through the Okanagan and the south coast to Vancouver Island, linking rail trails, greenways, and road sections across four regions. The northern route follows the Alaska Highway corridor about 1,031 km from Dawson Creek toward the Yukon border — the land connection between the rest of the Trans Canada Trail and the Arctic coast. Both are long-distance corridors best suited to experienced touring cyclists rather than casual day rides. 2 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. The full writeup, map, and directions live on Trans Canada Trail's website. body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / Great Northern Bikepacking Route Great Northern Bikepacking Route individual route creator visit → The Great Northern Bikepacking Route (GNBR) is a mostly off-road bikepacking route created by Ontario adventure cyclist and writer Matt Kadey, spanning over 13,000 km across 10 Canadian provinces and 3 U.S. states, from the Pacific to the Atlantic — one of the most ambitious route-mapping projects in the country. It is published segment by segment on a dedicated website, with route data on RideWithGPS and gear and provisioning notes alongside the maps. Their BC collection The British Columbia section of the GNBR is split into two long RideWithGPS routes covering roughly 1,770 km combined, from Vancouver-Coast and Mountains through the Thompson-Okanagan, Cariboo-Chilcotin Coast, and Kootenay-Rockies. Both are multi-day, high-climbing bikepacking routes on mixed surfaces, with Part Two mostly unpaved (67%) and Part One closer to an even paved/unpaved mix (47% unpaved). 2 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / Trans Canada Bike Route Network Trans Canada Bike Route Network route network visit → A volunteer-run, community-collaborative project mapping a proposed coast-to-coast National Cycling Route Network for Canada. It publishes route data as GPX files, a Garmin BaseCamp database (GDB) with points of interest, KMZ files for offline smartphone use, interactive Google Maps, and a curated Ride with GPS collection. How we describe routes → “When most people think of British Columbia, they picture towering, glacier-capped mountains and vast conifer forests. In the south-central part of the province, however, lies a unique and environmentally significant grassland landscape. B.C.’s grasslands make up just one percent of its land base but provide habitat for almost a third of the province’s threatened and endangered species, according to the Grasslands Conservation Council of British Columbia. This route is designed to explore part of this environmentally important landscape. It begins in Kamloops and will inspire with its great beauty. title: Frog Peak Loop
desc: Welcoming cycling stops, communities, and access along Frog Peak Loop, Kootenay Rockies — a ride described at BIKEPACKING.com.
body: Photo: BIKEPACKING.com Frog Peak Loop Home / Get Inspired / Kootenay Rockies / Frog Peak Loop Frog Peak Loop A ride described at BIKEPACKING.com Ambitious How we describe routes → Ambitious A real undertaking. Demanding on a couple of fronts, like rough surfaces plus steady climbing, or a long stretch on busier roads. Difficulty Our overall read of how demanding a route is. We score surface roughness, climbing, singletrack, and how far it runs from services. The route publisher's own rating, a lot of busy road riding, or sheer scale can push the tier up, never down. Derived from OpenStreetMap. Good data, not perfect. Spot something wrong? Tell us . How we describe routes → “The Frog Peak Loop is a non-technical and logistically straightforward gravel route, making it the perfect intro to bikepacking in the Kootenays. The official starting point is in Nelson, but it’s possible to start anywhere in the Slocan Valley or at the revered Frog Peak Café if you need a caffeine hit before you ride. At 107 kilometers (66 miles) long, the route can be tackled in a single day but is best enjoyed extended over a weekend to soak in the beauty of the West Kootenays. Despite feeling remote at times, this is offset by its proximity to small communities, delicious food stops, and well-traveled rail trails. If you’re looking for a route to convert the first-time bikepacker, this is it. The route has ample swimming spots, resupply points, and campgrounds, making it an ideal weekend trip.” — BIKE

body: Home / Field Notes / Calling everyone who loves exploring BC by bike! Calling everyone who loves exploring BC by bike! May 27, 2026 Lower Seymour Conservation Reserve, North Vancouver, BC The BC Cycle Tourism Society wants to make British Columbia an easier, safer, and more welcoming place to explore by bike. We're starting with building out practical information for riders, communities, and businesses. We'll share more soon about our plans and structure... but we don't want to wait until everything is finished before we start listening. A great bike trip is made of two pieces, right? A beautiful, interesting place. We have that covered: BC is incredible. The other piece? It's the people we meet along the way who so often create the magic. So we're starting with an invitation: we'd love to hear from you. Subscribe, and tell us what interests you # The simplest way to help right now is to sign up for the newsletter . Knowing there is an audience for this work helps when we talk with communities, tourism organizations, businesses, funders, and partners. It shows that people care about making BC a better place for cycle touring (which for us absolutely includes bikepacking, rail trail explorations, scenic road treks, and everything in between). Delta, BC When you subscribe, there's a place to tell us what interests you. Please do: a human reads every response. title: Every BC bike trip starts with the same questions. Not anymore.
desc: Quebec and Ontario figured this out. BC hadn't — until now. BC Bike Stops is a business directory built for what touring cyclists actually need to know.
body: Home / Field Notes / Every BC bike trip starts with the same questions. Not anymore. Every BC bike trip starts with the same questions. Not anymore. May 27, 2026 Whistler, BC When I planned my ride on the Sea to Sky Trail with my family, I had questions I couldn't fully answer from my desk. Would the hostels have somewhere to store our bikes inside overnight? Would the buses take three bikes? The Squamish Connector said two maximum. SkyLynx would take three but only bagged… what kind of bag, exactly? We found out, eventually. The Whistler hostel had a ski room. The Squamish hostel had locked cargo containers. The bus took all three bikes despite what the website said. I overnighted a bike bag from Amazon and packed my bike in a parking lot. Every answer required a phone call, an email, or a calculated guess. Every touring cyclist in BC is doing the same detective work. That's the problem BC Bike Stops is designed to fix. What we built, and why # Quebec figured this out a long time ago. Their Bienvenue cyclistes! program has been running for decades, and 31% of overnight cycle tourists in Quebec adapt their itinerary based on Bienvenue cyclistes! certification. Ontario By Bike has done the same since 2007 and now has over 1,600 certified businesses. BC has had pieces of this — GoByBike BC's directory among them — but nothing built for touring. Until now. title: HOW TO: Take your bike on a coach bus
desc: Coach buses are one of BC's most underrated tools for cycle tourists — economical, low-carbon, and they usually accept bikes. Here's how to pack and ride along.
body: Home / Field Notes / HOW TO: Take your bike on a coach bus HOW TO: Take your bike on a coach bus May 27, 2026 Vancouver Pacific Central Station, Vancouver, BC Coach buses are one of BC's most underrated tools for cycle tourists. They're economical, reasonably low-carbon, and they usually accept bikes. The right combination of bus and bike unlocks point-to-point touring without a car. Coach services in BC # eBus has the most extensive network for cyclists. BC stops include Vancouver, Surrey, Chilliwack, Hope, Merritt, Kamloops, Salmon Arm, Sicamous, Armstrong, Vernon, Kelowna, Revelstoke, Golden, Quesnel, Williams Lake, and Prince George. Bike fee: $30. Rider Express runs two BC-relevant routes: the Vancouver–Calgary corridor (Vancouver, Surrey, Abbotsford, Chilliwack, Hope, Merritt, Kamloops, Salmon Arm, Sicamous, Revelstoke, Golden) and a separate Kelowna–Salmon Arm route (Kelowna, Vernon, Armstrong, Enderby, Salmon Arm). Bike fee: $60, or $50 if booked online in advance. YVR Skylynx runs Vancouver to Squamish to Whistler. One bike per passenger is free. All three of these operators require your bike to be in a bag or box for transport, which we cover below. IslandLink unfortunately DOES NOT ACCEPT BIKES . BC also has several regional coach and shuttle operators... many of them don't require special bike handling, just show up with your bike and put it on the rack. title: HOW TO: Keep your drivetrain happy on a multi-day ride
desc: Mat from Trip Longer cleans his chain every night on tour, and it takes five minutes. Here's his routine.
body: Home / Field Notes / HOW TO: Keep your drivetrain happy on a multi-day ride HOW TO: Keep your drivetrain happy on a multi-day ride July 27, 2026 Five minutes of care at the end of each riding day keeps your bike shifting smoothly for the whole trip. Mat Leblanc of Trip Longer filmed his nightly routine at camp, and it's the best short demo of trail-side drivetrain care we've seen: View this reel by @trip.longer on Instagram The routine # As Mat runs it: Prop the bike so the pedals can spin freely. Wipe down the chain with a rag. He keeps his in a ziplock bag so it doesn't dirty everything else. Get the derailleur's jockey wheels and the front chainring while you're in there. Shake the chain lube well, find the master link so you know where you started, and give every link a dab. Backspin the pedals about a dozen times to work the lube in. One last wipe of the chain, then let it sit overnight. Ready to ride in the morning. Why bother? Dust and chain lube mix into a fine grinding paste that wears out cassettes and chainrings surprisingly fast. A nightly wipe-and-lube costs you five minutes and saves your gear, especially on BC's gravel and rail trails. About Mat and Ali # Mat Leblanc and Ali Becker are the West Kootenay couple behind Trip Longer. title: HOW TO: Take your bike in a taxi or rideshare
desc: No bike rack required. With a little prep, a bagged bike rides fine in a cab, an Uber, or a Coastal Rides car.
body: Home / Field Notes / HOW TO: Take your bike in a taxi or rideshare HOW TO: Take your bike in a taxi or rideshare July 27, 2026 Sometimes the last 10 km are the hard ones. The bus depot is across town, the ferry leaves early, a wheel died, or the forecast turned. Good news: every bike that has ever ridden happily in a cab got there the same way: the driver knew it was coming, and the bike looked easy. That's the whole trick. Two moves. Both halves of one travel day: the taxi and the bus it was catching. Kamloops, BC Move one: tell them early # Drivers say no to surprises, not to bikes. Give the heads-up before anyone is standing at the curb. For taxis, skip the app and phone the dispatcher. When I tried to order a van through the taxi app in Kamloops it took ages to confirm; one phone call later a car was there in 10 minutes, and my bagged bike rode flat in the back of an ordinary Toyota Prius v wagon, backpacks and me along too. Say this on the phone: "I have a bike, packed small and clean, and one passenger. I need a car it'll fit in, like a hatchback please." Ready for pickup Uride's options in Kamloops, July 2026: an XL tier and a Pickup Notes field For app rides, pick a large car (see below) then use the text fields. Uride has a Pickup Notes box right on the booking screen, so the driver knows before they accept. On Uber or Lyft, message the driver once the ride matches. Message this in the app: "I have a clean bike and one passenger, ok?" We've never had a driver decline

title: BC road rules are being rewritten
desc: BC is consulting on changes to the Motor Vehicle Act. Most of the attention goes to city streets. Here are five proposed changes that matter most when you're touring.
body: Home / Field Notes / BC road rules are being rewritten BC road rules are being rewritten July 29, 2026 Gitwinksihlkw, BC · Photo: Marcus Paladino You're descending into Hope on Highway 3. A truck passes at 110 km/h, close enough to feel. Whether that pass is safe, legal, or enforceable depends on BC's Motor Vehicle Act (MVA), a law written mostly with cars in mind. That law is being rewritten. The province amended it in 2024 to require a minimum passing distance, and consultations on the next round of changes are underway now. Two BC cycling organizations, HUB Cycling and the BC Cycling Coalition, have put forward 25 recommendations for what those changes should be. Their highest-priority recommendations are strong: 30 km/h default limits on neighbourhood streets, no right turns on red, and a three-second following distance behind people on bikes. We read all 25 with a different rider in mind. Not the commuter on Commercial Drive, but the person three days into a loaded tour, on a rural highway, crossing a rail corridor, rolling into a town they've never seen. Cycle tourists spend long days on roads where there are no protected bike lanes, only the choices made by the people driving around them. Some of the recommendations that matter most for that rider sit well down the urban priority list. Here are our five. body: Home / Field Notes / May/June 2026 Dispatch BC Cycle Tourism Society The Field Notes Dispatch May/June 2026 Issue #1 · Monthly newsletter on cycle tourism in British Columbia Welcome to the inaugural issue of The Field Notes Dispatch . The BC Cycle Tourism Society wants to make British Columbia an easier, safer, and more welcoming place to explore by bike. We're starting with building out practical information for riders, communities, and businesses — and we're starting by listening. A great bike trip is made of two pieces, right? A beautiful, interesting place — we have that covered, BC is incredible. The other piece is the people we meet along the way. So we're starting with an invitation: we'd love to hear from you. Read the full hello → The Feature Every BC bike trip starts with the same questions. Not anymore. # May 27, 2026 Whistler, BC When I planned my ride on the Sea to Sky Trail with my family, I had questions I couldn't fully answer from my desk. Would the hostels have somewhere to store our bikes inside overnight? Would the buses take three bikes? The Squamish Connector said two maximum. SkyLynx would take three but only bagged… what kind of bag, exactly? We found out, eventually. The Whistler hostel had a ski room. The Squamish hostel had locked cargo containers. The bus took all three bikes despite what the website said. I overnighted a bike bag from Amazon and packed my bike in a parking lot. Every answer required a phone call, an email, or a calculated guess.

title: About
desc: About the BC Cycle Tourism Society — a nonprofit organization supporting cycle tourism and bikepacking across British Columbia.
body: Home / About About the BC Cycle Tourism Society British Columbia has some of the world's most spectacular cycling terrain: rail trails through mountain valleys, coastal routes along the Pacific, wine country roads, rainforest paths, and gravel that goes on forever. What it has been missing is a provincial organization to help turn these remarkable cycling assets into a coherent, connected, and world-class visitor experience. That's what the BC Cycle Tourism Society is building. We incorporated in spring 2026 as a new nonprofit provincial cycle tourism organization working to build the marketing, standards, partnerships, and policy environment that can help cycle tourism and bikepacking thrive across British Columbia. Our goal is to grow cycle tourism as a meaningful economic opportunity for rural communities, tourism organizations, local businesses, and BC as a whole. BC Cycle Tourism Society (Society number S0085454) grew out of several organizations already working to make cycling, trails, and active transportation stronger in British Columbia: The BC Cycling Coalition, Trails BC, and Let's Go Biking. The Society is building an Advisory Council with regional knowledge and sector experience. We're a regional organization member of the Outdoor Recreation Council of BC (ORCBC), and a sector association member of the Tourism Industry Association of BC (TIABC). We look to places like New Zealand and Québec as models: jurisdictions that invested in coordinated route networks, des

title: Advocacy
desc: What BC Cycle Tourism Society advocates for: getting there with a bike, e-bikes, safe roads between communities, protecting rail corridors and resource road access, measuring the cycle tourism economy, and tourism that respects place. Includes our Sea-to-Sky rail corridor reports and the Kettle Valley Rail Trail.
body: Home / Advocacy Advocacy Cycle touring depends on a lot of decisions that happen in meeting rooms: whether an old rail corridor is kept in one piece, whether a washed-out trail gets repair money, whether a bus takes bikes. Those decisions often get made without anyone in the room who travels by bike. Our goal is to change that, so the benefits and interests of cycle tourism in BC are considered. We come at this as a tourism economic development organization, and it shapes how we advocate. We do the research first, publish it openly, and offer it to the people making the decision. We are a young organization, so some of what follows is what we do today, and more of it is what we plan to do as we grow. The datasets and reports behind the work we have already done are on our Research and Data page. Here is what we care about, in three groups: the journey itself, the corridors and trails it runs on, and growing cycle tourism well. The journey # Getting there with a bike. A trip only works if the bike can reach the start and get home from the finish. We publish what every ferry, bus, train, and airline in BC actually does with bikes, so riders and operators are working from the same information. As we grow, we plan to work with carriers on capacity, packaging rules, and reservable bike spaces. E-bikes. title: No turn-away camping
desc: Campgrounds that always find room for someone arriving by bike. The January 2026 letter from seven cycling and outdoor recreation organizations to Metro Vancouver Regional Parks, with the evidence behind it.
body: Home / Advocacy / No turn-away camping No turn-away camping Photo: Heather Piwowar The single most useful thing a campground can do for cycle tourism costs almost nothing: promise that someone who arrives by bike will always be found somewhere to sleep, even when every site is booked. In January 2026, seven cycling and outdoor recreation organizations asked Metro Vancouver Regional Parks to adopt exactly that, as part of its Regional Parks Camping Opportunities Study. Four more organizations sent letters of support, including Destination British Columbia and Trans Canada Trail. Why cyclists need it # A cyclist cannot camp the way a driver can. Weather, fatigue, injury, and mechanical trouble make it hard to commit to a date months ahead, which is what a reservation system asks for. Arriving early to claim a first-come, first-served site is hard when you spend the day riding. And if the campground is full at the end of a long day, riding another 40 km is not a small adjustment. There are practical differences too. A cyclist has no car trunk to keep food away from animals. Distance is the constraint that shapes everything, so sites in many parks matter more than lots of sites in one park. None of this is unusual or extreme. It is what self-contained cycle touring is normally like. The 2025 Metro Vancouver camping study did not consider it at all. What the letter asks for # 1. Adopt a no turn-away policy. title: Land Acknowledgement
desc: Land Acknowledgement for the BC Cycle Tourism Society website.
body: Home / Land acknowledgement Land Acknowledgement The cycling routes and communities featured on this website are located throughout what is now British Columbia, on many First Nations territories, including unceded and treaty lands. We acknowledge the enduring relationships, rights, laws, cultures, and stewardship responsibilities of First Nations in these places. As this network grows, we are committed to listening and building respectful relationships with Indigenous communities whose territories and priorities are connected to cycle tourism in BC. We're also committed to deepening our understanding of the history and present-day stories of the peoples whose lands we ride through, and we encourage our readers to do the same. Tools such as Native Land and Whose Land can be useful starting points.

If you ride these trails, support the trail organizations . The routes we feature were designed by real people who scouted, mapped, and documented them. Meet the route makers . Riding in BC keeps getting better because bike advocacy organizations have spent decades building bike-friendly culture, laws, and infrastructure.
